disguise: *** THE PAGE THAT COUNTS BEFORE IT HAS LOOKED ***
what it looked like: *** "Historical Record Search Results (0)" *** - complete, composed, confident, and indistinguishable from an empty result.
what it actually was: The heading rendering *** while the query was still running. *** Waiting returned the five records, then 210, then 822.
how it was caught: A control on *** Sancho Lerena ***, whose five records had been pulled twenty minutes earlier, returned zero as well. A known-false zero proves the fault is in the query.

disguise: *** AND IT IS STILL DOING IT SIX DAYS LATER ***
what it looked like: The same "(0)", three times in one sitting - on Justo, on Alfredo Justiniano, and on the first Gilberto sweep.
what it actually was: *** 39, 80 and 63 records. *** The heading is the page talking to itself before the results arrive.
how it was caught: Reading the page *** twice ***, which is in this archive's habits precisely because of the entry above, and still nearly produced three false nulls in one evening.

disguise: *** THE SESSION THAT LOGGED ITSELF OUT AND DID NOT SAY SO ***
what it looked like: Three searches returning zero results *** and no "No Results Found" line *** - which is normally this archive's proof that a search ran.
what it actually was: The FamilySearch session had *** silently expired *** and every request was being redirected to ident.familysearch.org, the sign-in page. It does not announce a logout, and the page that arrives is not obviously an error.
how it was caught: The control, *** and only the control: *** "Sancho Lerena", which had returned three Canelones baptisms, returned nothing.

disguise: *** THE QUOTA ERROR WEARING AN EMPTY SHELF ***
what it looked like: A Google Books API response reading *** totalItems: None. ***
what it actually was: *** An HTTP 429 *** - the quota refusing, not the shelf being bare.
how it was caught: The status code, which the body never mentioned.

disguise: *** THE BLOCK BEHIND AN EMPTY BODY ***
what it looked like: A zero-length response, no error, no message.
what it actually was: *** "Access Denied - Error 15, this request was blocked by our security service" *** - delivered as an empty body rather than as a refusal.
how it was caught: The same class of failure as the quota error: *** the service failing in a way that resembles success. *** Worse than an outage, because an outage announces itself.

disguise: *** THE ZERO DELIVERED ON THE WAY TO A BLOCK ***
what it looked like: A clean-looking zero from the Granada index, moments before Error 15 arrived.
what it actually was: A search already being refused. *** "A zero delivered immediately before a block is the least trustworthy zero there is." ***
how it was caught: The control - *** "Juan de Lerena y Aguilar", a phrase known to return a hit because it was read an hour before *** - never loaded at all.

disguise: *** THE THROTTLE THAT EMPTIES A PAGE ***
what it looked like: Four consecutive image transcripts returning *** length zero *** - which looks exactly like four blank pages in a register.
what it actually was: *** Rate limiting. *** Image 86, re-read after a forty-second pause, gave 2,970 characters. Image 22 had failed three times across two days and read clean at 3,451.
how it was caught: A zero is never allowed to count as a read. *** Eleven pages would otherwise have been silently certified as empty. ***

disguise: *** AND THE EMPTY PAGE THAT WAS NOT THE THROTTLE ***
what it looked like: Three more empty transcripts, identical in every visible way to the throttle above.
what it actually was: *** Images outside the volume altogether. *** The film holds 421 images and several volumes, not the 148 assumed.
how it was caught: *** The page TITLE. *** A throttled page still resolves to the volume's name; an image outside the volume resolves to something else. Without that check the three would have been logged "not read" forever and the volume never called finished.

disguise: *** THE QUERY THAT CANNOT REACH WHAT IS THERE ***
what it looked like: Two exact-surname searches returning zero *** with *** the "No Results Found" line present.
what it actually was: The indexed surname was a *** compound - "Lerena y Armenta" - *** which exact matching will not reach.
how it was caught: A control showed the same query shape could not retrieve a record *** known to be in the collection. A null from a query that cannot find what is there is not a null. ***

disguise: *** THE COUNT THAT HAS NO ZERO TO GIVE ***
what it looked like: The FamilySearch *** personas API *** answering 8,549 for surname Lerena in Uruguay.
what it actually was: *** The same 8,549 for every variant *** - add a given name, add a spouse, change the control's parameters entirely. The field ignores them. An invented surname, Zzzqqxx, still returns *** 102. ***
how it was caught: Running a control with *** deliberately different parameters *** and getting an identical number. No null can ever be drawn from an instrument that cannot return one.

disguise: *** THE COLLECTION FILED UNDER THE WRONG COUNTRY ***
what it looked like: A reel whose page title attributes it to *** COLOMBIA. ***
what it actually was: *** Uruguayan acts. *** The attribution is simply wrong on FamilySearch's side.
how it was caught: Reading the images rather than the label. *** Recorded because a researcher who trusted the page title would conclude the reel is Colombian and abandon it. ***

disguise: *** THE CORPUS THAT HOLDS THE WRONG RECORD TYPE ***
what it looked like: Spanish full-text searches for *** Felix Llerena and Rosalia Aguilar *** returning zero.
what it actually was: The Andalusian full-text corpus holds *** nobility and notarial records, not parish registers. *** The zero meant "not findable by this instrument", not "not there".
how it was caught: Asking the control question - *** what Andalusian collections exist at all *** - instead of asking for the name again. Until the corpus is mapped, every Spanish null this archive produces is uninterpretable.

disguise: *** AND AGAIN THE NEXT DAY, ON A COUPLE WHOSE CHILDREN ARE IN THIS REGISTER ***
what it looked like: A parent-pair query on *** BERNABE LERENA and CASIMIRA PELAEZ ***, whose four children this archive has held since 13 September.
what it actually was: *** "(0)" ON THE FIRST READ AND 22 ON THE SECOND. *** Four seconds apart.
how it was caught: *** THE ONLY REASON IT WAS CAUGHT IS THAT THE ANSWER WAS ALREADY KNOWN TO BE WRONG *** - the same thing that caught the very first one on 14 September. A control you happen to be standing on.

disguise: *** A PARENT'S SURNAME THAT REMOVES THE RECORDS IT MATCHES ***
what it looked like: A parent-pair query on *** AVELINO LERENA and CELEDONIA VILLADEMOROS ***, Uruguay - father's surname exact, mother's given name and surname supplied - returned a clean *** 0 ***, with rows rendered and the page settled. Read twice.
what it actually was: *** SEVEN RECORDS, AND TWO OF THEM ARE IN THIS REGISTER ALREADY *** - the christenings of Avelino Pedro Joaquin Silvestre in 1866 and Pedro Gualberto in 1870. *** Deleting the mother's SURNAME and keeping only 'Celedonia' returned all seven. *** The likely mechanism: the mother's whole name sits unparsed in the given-name field, so supplying a surname excludes every record the parser failed on - and one of the seven displays its mother as 'Celedonia Villademoros', spelled exactly as asked.
how it was caught: *** THE ARCHIVE'S OWN RECORDS. *** The zero was known to be wrong before it was investigated, because this couple's children were entered on 20 September. *** No control would have caught it: *** the control for this shape - Alberto Lerena with Maria Ines Larriera - had returned sixteen records in the same session, which is what made the zero look trustworthy.

disguise: *** THE SAME TRAP AGAIN, ONE HOUR LATER, AND THIS TIME THE RULE CAUGHT IT ***
what it looked like: A parent-pair query on *** ALFREDO LERENA and HERMENEGILDA GAVARRO ***, Uruguay: *** 0 ***.
what it actually was: *** THREE RECORDS. *** Deleting the mother's SURNAME and keeping only 'Hermenegilda' returned them - and they are her own death registration of 1940, which the archive had never seen. *** The index writes her surname 'Navarro de Terenadel', a machine mangling of GAVAZZO DE LERENA ***, so no spelling anybody would have guessed could have reached her.
how it was caught: *** BY THE RULE WRITTEN DOWN SIXTY MINUTES EARLIER: delete each added parameter in turn. *** The Villademoros zero cost an afternoon and was caught only because the archive already held the hidden records. This one cost one query. *** That is the whole argument for writing the rule down instead of remembering it. ***

disguise: *** THE ONE THAT PASSED EVERY TEST THIS ARCHIVE HAS ***
what it looked like: *** EVERY SEARCH RETURNING 0. *** Not a slow page and not an error: 'Historical Record Search Results (0)' with *** 'No Results Found' *** printed beneath it - the POSITIVE ASSERTION OF EMPTINESS this archive treats as the mark of a real null - *** stable across two reads twelve seconds apart, and still 0 after a NINETY-SECOND wait. ***
what it actually was: *** ONE BROWSER CONTEXT LOST ITS AUTH, AND ONLY ONE. *** First the arithmetic: *** surname GONZALEZ in URUGUAY returned 0 ***, in a collection running to millions, and the same URL that returned TEN records that morning returned 0 that afternoon. Then the apparent cause: full-text, asked the same question, *** REDIRECTED TO THE SIGN-IN PAGE ***. *** THAT LOOKED LIKE AN EXPIRED ACCOUNT AND WAS NOT. *** A sibling archive on the same machine ran both searches in the same minutes and got 3,652 and 3,967 with the account name in the nav bar. *** Each session's in-app browser is its own browser with its own cookie jar; one lost its auth and recovered by itself. *** In a FRESH TAB the same Gonzalez query returned *** 479,662 *** and Avelino with Ambrosia returned *** 10 *** again. *** THE RECORD SEARCH STILL NEVER SAID SO: it answered 0 with 'No Results Found' throughout, where full-text in the same context said plainly that it had no session. ***
how it was caught: *** BY A CONTROL WHOSE ANSWER CANNOT BE ZERO. *** Every other guard failed: the count was stable, the 'No Results Found' line was present, the wait was long, and a control run EARLIER THE SAME DAY had passed. *** THE ARCHIVE WAS ONE STEP FROM PUBLISHING A FABRICATED MECHANISM *** - that the parent-pair query cannot reach acts held only in full text - built entirely on this outage. *** SO THE RULE GAINS TWO WORDS: a control must be RECENT, and its answer must be ARITHMETICALLY IMPOSSIBLE TO BE ZERO. *** *** AND A FREE TEST THAT COSTS ONE NAVIGATION: ask the FULL-TEXT search anything. It admits a lost session; the record search hides one behind a null. *** *** BUT THE REMEDY IS NOT WHAT THIS ARCHIVE FIRST SAID. *** It published that the account was signed out and that David would have to sign in again. *** Wrong, and corrected within the hour: open a new tab, or check another session's browser, before asking a person to do anything. *** The three nulls held over for re-testing - Luis with Carolina, Carlos with Luisa, Juan Arturo with Isidora - were all re-run against a live control and all three are still zero, so nothing was lost but the afternoon.

disguise: *** A PARENT-PAIR SEARCH THAT NEEDS A SURNAME AND WILL NOT SAY SO ***
what it looked like: *** SANCHO as father with MARIA as mother, Uruguay: 0. *** Read twice, with a live control - Gonzalez in Uruguay returning 479,660 minutes earlier.
what it actually was: *** THE QUERY SHAPE, NOT THE FAMILY. *** The arithmetic settles it without any judgement: *** father given name SANCHO alone returns 10,315. Mother given name MARIA alone returns 1,228,708. Together they return 0. *** Two fields matching five and seven figures cannot intersect at nothing in a country where Maria is the commonest name a mother has. *** ADD THE TWO SURNAMES - Llerena and Fernandez - AND THE SAME QUERY RETURNS SIX, every one of them real. ***
how it was caught: *** BY ARITHMETIC, WHICH IS THE ONLY GUARD THAT HAS NEVER FAILED HERE. *** The rule this yields is worth more than the instance: *** a parent-pair query with GIVEN NAMES ONLY returns zero whatever the truth is, so at least one parent SURNAME must be supplied before any null from this shape means anything. *** Every earlier zero in this archive drawn from given names alone is void; every one drawn with a surname stands.
